concept.name: Real GDP
concept.definition: Gross domestic product adjusted to remove the effects of price changes, so that output in different periods can be compared in constant purchasing-power terms. When media report 'GDP growth' they almost always mean the percent change in real GDP.
concept.intuition: Real GDP answers: did the country actually produce more stuff, or did prices just go up? It strips out inflation so growth reflects volume, not price changes.
concept.mechanics: BEA deflates each component of nominal spending using detailed price indexes (producing chained-dollar estimates), so real GDP changes reflect changes in quantities produced. Growth rates are computed from these chained series, seasonally adjusted at annual rates.
concept.formula: Real GDP = Nominal GDP / GDP price index x 100 (conceptually); in practice BEA uses chained (Fisher) quantity indexes rather than a single deflator.
concept.failure_modes: Deflation choices and base-year/index updates can revise history; real GDP can rise while living standards for typical households stagnate if gains accrue narrowly or population grows faster.
concept.misconceptions: Real GDP is not 'GDP with inflation subtracted at the CPI'; BEA uses its own chain-type price indexes, so the implied GDP deflator differs from CPI inflation.
concept.example: If nominal GDP rises 5% but prices rise 3%, real GDP rises roughly 2% — the growth that economists and the Fed treat as actual output growth.

citations.source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis — Gross Domestic Product (Learning Center)
